claims.text: Every physical quantity consists of a numerical magnitude and a unit: the unit names the standard the magnitude is counted against, and together they state the value of the quantity.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The same magnitude with a different unit states a different value: 1.5 km and 1.5 m are different lengths, because the unit is part of the value, so a magnitude written without its unit is incomplete.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A reasonable estimate states a magnitude with its unit, judged without measuring directly and expected to lie within about a power of ten of the actual value.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Known reference magnitudes anchor estimates: an adult person has a mass of about 70 kg, a car on a main road travels at about 25 m s⁻¹, and a door is about 2.0 m tall.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: An estimate is checked by comparing it with a reference quantity of the same kind: a candidate mass of 6 kg for an adult fails against the reference 70 kg, and 60 kg passes.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The SI base quantities and their units are mass (kilogram, kg), length (metre, m), time (second, s), electric current (ampere, A), temperature (kelvin, K) and amount of substance (mole, mol); the five named for recall are the first five of this set.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A base quantity is one of the quantities the others are built from, and a base unit is its unit: the kilogram is the unit of the base quantity mass, not the quantity itself, and charge is a derived quantity, not a base quantity.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Answering with base units (kg, A) or with a derived quantity such as charge when base quantities are asked for confuses units with quantities; the test is whether each item in the answer is a quantity or a unit.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A derived unit is written as a product or quotient of SI base units: force has N = kg m s⁻², pressure has Pa = kg m⁻¹ s⁻² and energy has J = kg m² s⁻².

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The unit of a derived quantity follows from its defining equation: since p = F/A, pressure has the unit N/m², which in base units is kg m⁻¹ s⁻², given the name pascal (Pa).

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: An answer required in base units must contain base units only: leaving a unit such as N, Pa or J in the answer leaves the conversion unfinished; the test is whether the final unit contains base units only.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: An equation is homogeneous when every term in it carries the same SI base units, so that the two sides can be equated and the terms added.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: To test homogeneity, write each symbol in base units and compare both sides: in v² = u² + 2as, the terms v² and u² are m² s⁻² and the term 2as is m s⁻² × m = m² s⁻², so the equation is homogeneous.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Homogeneity is necessary for a physical equation to be correct, not sufficient: an equation with a wrong number in front, such as F = 2ma, is still homogeneous, because a pure number carries no units.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The prefixes are pico (p, 10⁻¹²), nano (n, 10⁻⁹), micro (µ, 10⁻⁶), milli (m, 10⁻³), centi (c, 10⁻²), deci (d, 10⁻¹), kilo (k, 10³), mega (M, 10⁶), giga (G, 10⁹) and tera (T, 10¹²).

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Prefixed values are converted to base units before substituting: 250 mA is 0.25 A, 2.0 GHz is 2.0 × 10⁹ Hz and 4.0 mm² is 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ m².

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A slipped power of ten in a prefix conversion most often comes from a factor not squared: an area in mm² is multiplied by 10⁻⁶ to give m², because the millimetre and the square both convert; the test is whether every value is in base units before substituting.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A systematic error shifts every reading of the same measurement by the same amount or in the same direction; a zero error, where an instrument reads a non-zero value before anything is measured, is a common systematic error.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A random error is an unpredictable scatter of readings about the mean; repeating and averaging reduces its effect, because the scatter partly cancels, and the mean of repeated readings is a better estimate of the true value.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Repeating readings and averaging reduces random error only; a systematic error such as a zero error shifts every reading the same way and survives any number of repeats, so it must be corrected at its source: zero the instrument or subtract the offset. The test is whether the error pushes every reading in the same direction.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Accuracy is how close a measured value is to the true value; precision is how close repeated readings are to each other, and also the smallest division a reading is recorded to.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A set of readings can be precise and inaccurate at once: the readings may agree closely with each other while a systematic error shifts all of them away from the true value; the test is whether the readings could agree closely and all be wrong.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The absolute uncertainty of a value is the range either side of it within which the true value is expected to lie, in the unit of the quantity: half the smallest division of the instrument for one reading, and half the range for repeated readings.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Uncertainties combine by simple addition: sums and differences of quantities add their absolute uncertainties, and products and quotients add their percentage (or fractional) uncertainties.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The percentage uncertainty of a value is its absolute uncertainty divided by the value itself, multiplied by 100.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A quantity raised to the power n contributes n times its own percentage uncertainty, so d² contributes twice the percentage uncertainty in d and d³ three times; adding absolute uncertainties for a product or quotient, or treating a percentage uncertainty as an absolute one, is the error. The test is whether the derived quantity is found by adding or subtracting, or by multiplying or dividing, and what power each measured quantity carries.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A scalar quantity has magnitude only, such as mass, speed, distance, energy, work, power, pressure, charge, time or temperature; a vector quantity has magnitude and direction, such as displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight or momentum.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The test between the two is whether reversing the direction changes the quantity: for a vector it does, and a scalar has no direction to reverse.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Work, energy, power, pressure and charge are scalars even though vectors appear in their defining equations; calling them vectors is the error, and the test is whether reversing the direction changes the quantity.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Two coplanar vectors add by the triangle method (the second starts where the first ends, and the resultant runs from the start of the first to the end of the second) or by the parallelogram; a vector is subtracted by adding its reverse, A − B = A + (−B).

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Two perpendicular vectors of magnitudes x and y give a resultant of magnitude √(x² + y²), at an angle θ to the first, where tan θ = y ÷ x.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: For two vectors of magnitudes P and Q at any other angle θ between them, the resultant magnitude comes from R² = P² + Q² + 2PQ cos θ.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A vector V at an angle θ to a reference direction resolves into two perpendicular components: V cos θ along the reference direction and V sin θ perpendicular to it, where θ is the angle between the vector and the reference direction.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Swapping sine and cosine when resolving is the error: the component alongside the angle is V cos θ and the component opposite the angle is V sin θ; the test is whether the wanted component is next to the angle or opposite it.

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Resolving is the reverse of adding perpendicular vectors: the components V cos θ and V sin θ recombine to the original vector, because (V cos θ)² + (V sin θ)² = V².

verification.method: Authored for 9702 topic 1 (Physical quantities and units) under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).
